cim: How To Govern Artificial Intelligence Without Government
cim_eredeti: How To Govern Artificial Intelligence Without Government
szoveg_eredeti:
Bill Gates—who definitely knows a thing or two about software—recently told NBC's Meet the Press that "AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths." Indeed, this risk was presaged in 2023 by hundreds of AI experts who signed the Statement on AI Extinction Risk, declaring that mitigating that risk "should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel laureate, put it plainly: "Anybody who says it's all going to be fine, it's crazy."

The same experts see extraordinary promise. AI systems are already attacking famously unsolved problems in mathematics, and breakthroughs in medicine and science are certain to follow.

With few exceptions, there is an expert consensus that AI must be governed, both to reduce its risks and to fulfill its amazing promise.

The people building AI agree. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warns that AI could cause humanity to "lose control of the future." Anthropic's S-1 notes that “a wide range of stakeholders, including researchers and policymakers, have raised concerns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls for "regulation of AI," and Altman agrees that consistent rules for frontier risk "are a good idea." Demis Hassabis, CEO of DeepMind, likewise calls for the creation of a “standards body.” The two other major American firms competing to win the race for the best AI products—SpaceX (which acquired xAI in February) and Meta—have been less explicit publicly. But in April more than 600 Google employees urged CEO Sundar Pichai to keep the company’s AI out of classified Pentagon work, citing its “most unethical and dangerous uses.” In September, a former Google DeepMind safety researcher, Bilal Chughtai, warned that AI “has the potential to kill us all.”

In a fiercely competitive sector where hundreds of billions of dollars are invested each year, no single firm can adopt a regulatory paradigm on its own and thereby eliminate risks or maximize benefits. Nor would stifling competition or anointing a national champion serve innovation or growth.

The problem then is not whether to regulate AI, but how to do so while achieving three goals: avoiding catastrophe while preserving competition, and maximizing public benefits.

Lawmakers in the 119th Congress have introduced nearly 600 AI-related bills, from the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Safety Act to the bipartisan FRONTIER Act. But given the executive branch’s current opposition to regulation, none are likely to pass over the next two years.

Nor is the executive branch authoring, as yet, a proposal for a new government agency with the capacity to achieve those three goals. Instead, President Trump created the Super Intelligence Force, a task force led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and co-chaired by OPM Director Scott Kupor, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, and Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael. It has 120 days to recommend the federal government's role. But it does not have the structure that would enable it to address the concerns many have raised on an ongoing basis.

Moreover, in less than 90 days a new Congress will be sworn in. If the recent past is prologue, the prospect of reasonable consensus between Congressional thinking on the AI governance problem and the Executive Branch’s ideas may be fanciful.

But we cannot wait another two years in the hopes of another election providing an appropriate consensus. We need to start addressing the risks associated with AI now.

Under these circumstances, the nation’s great and well-endowed nonprofit foundations should provide the way forward. American nonprofits have a long record of building new institutions for new problems. The track record includes:

While the government often assisted in the creation and strengthened these efforts in various ways, the key driver was the non-profit sector.

This moment calls for the same move toward good governance but away from government.

Major charitable foundations—joined by philanthropies from the right, the left, and from the tech world—should establish and endow an independent institution to govern frontier AI. The nonprofit corporation would not tax the AI firms, and the firms would not govern it. (For more detail, see the full proposal here.)

The foundations would fund it and choose its governing board. That board’s members should have true expertise, absolutely no economic stake in any AI firm, and explicit authority to choose their own successors, so the institution never depends on the goodwill of its founders or of the firms it oversees.

They should be paid and plan to serve at least two staggered five-year terms. The sectors that buy AI services, including health care, finance, education, energy, and state and local government, should have a formal advisory role.

The board could choose to work with the Standards Authority for Frontier AI, the self-regulatory body Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are now planning, but the nonprofit would make its own decisions. In technical talent and agility, it would resemble the “self-regulatory organisation” proposed by Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, but the critical difference between that body and what we are proposing is that our entity would be funded and run independently. While the industry body may be sincere in its efforts, independence will be key to building and earning public trust.

The new institution would do three things. First, it would evaluate the models of every major AI firm and rate them on safety, transparency, data protection and other factors. (This has precedent in far more benign settings. In 1968, the movie industry, with Jack Valenti's help, created its own rating system, and films have carried ratings that theaters have enforced ever since.) If hospitals, banks, schools, governments and other major institutions and sectors committed to buying only top-rated models, market forces would drive a race to the top.

A good rating would also improve an AI firm's ability to buy insurance and to defend itself against product liability lawsuits. Those suits could someday cost the industry hundreds of billions of dollars, or substantially all of its profits. Underwriters and juries alike would treat an independent safety rating as evidence of reasonable care.

Second, through independent governance, the institution would preserve competition. A credible rating depends on detailed, current information about each company’s models. If competing AI firms shared that information directly with one another, or met to agree among themselves on what counts as safe, they would risk antitrust charges of collusion, and the public would have reason to worry that “safety standards” were really a way for incumbents to shut out rivals. The independent nonprofit would keep each firm’s data in confidence, keep it walled off from competitors, and determine its own methodology. Drawing on precedent from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety and National Commission for Quality Assurance, firms would compete to earn the best rating rather than coordinate behind closed doors.

Third, the corporation would issue advisory opinions on where the industry should cooperate to provide new public goods at low or even zero cost. AI may yield new vaccines, new treatments, and scientific breakthroughs that no single firm can profitably give away. An independent body could identify those opportunities and set the terms on which competitors share the work and the results. Biohub’s Virtual Biology Initiative—backed by the National Institutes of Health, the Energy Department, Meta, and Google DeepMind—has grown to $1.8 billion to use AI to create better treatments for human diseases.
